passage: Pickup note, Thursday. Saurabh's painting tore as he ran out, and he flung himself on the mat, sobbing. His mother, Chandrika, snapped first: "Get up, we're late!" Then she stopped, knelt beside him and waited. "You're sad your rocket ripped. I shouted just now, and I'm sorry." He leaned into her. They taped the rocket together on the bench. I have seen her lose patience before, and I have seen her come back every time; he still runs to her. Next step: I gave them extra tape for home.

qa.q: What happened to Saurabh's painting?
qa.a: Saurabh's painting tore as he ran out.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling on the mat, and how did it change?
qa.a: He was upset and sad about his ripped rocket; once his mother knelt, named it and said sorry, he seemed comforted and leaned into her.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do after snapping that other parents could copy?
qa.a: She stopped, knelt, named Saurabh's sadness and apologised for shouting, which turned a slip into a repair.

qa.q: How does the note-writer see Chandrika as a parent?
qa.a: The note-writer sees that she is not perfect and loses patience, but she comes back every time, which is why Saurabh still runs to her.

grounding: Shows a parent who snaps, then repairs, names her child's sadness and stays calmly beside him.

passage: The anganwadi gate was already shut when Saurabh's father, Kamal, came running from the sugarcane field. Saurabh stood by the helper, face wet, fists tight. Kamal crouched in the dust. "You were frightened I wasn't coming. I was late, and that was my mistake." Saurabh hit his shoulder once, then climbed into his lap. Kamal didn't scold. He just held him till the hiccups slowed. On the walk home past the pond, Saurabh made him promise: "Tomorrow, early." Kamal tied a red thread on his own wrist to remember.

qa.q: Where was Kamal coming from when he reached the anganwadi?
qa.a: He came running from the sugarcane field.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh hit Kamal's shoulder and then climb into his lap?
qa.a: He was frightened and angry that his father was late, yet he still trusted him enough to seek comfort from him.

qa.q: What did Kamal do that helped Saurabh settle?
qa.a: He crouched down, named the fear, admitted the lateness was his mistake and held Saurabh without scolding until he calmed.

qa.q: What would change if Kamal had scolded Saurabh for crying?
qa.a: Saurabh might learn that his fear is not welcome and feel less safe turning to his father the next time he is scared.

grounding: Illustrates a parent staying calm, naming a child's fear and owning his own mistake of arriving late.

passage: Thunder cracked over the flats in Haifa, and Noa, five, shrieked from her bed. Her father, Yosef, half asleep, called out, "It's only noise, go to sleep!" The crying got louder. He sighed, padded in and sat on the floor beside her. "That was a big bang. You got scared, and I answered too fast. Sorry." Noa peeked out from the blanket. He counted with her between each flash and rumble, slowly. By the last flash she was counting on her own, one hand still holding his sleeve.

qa.q: Where did Yosef sit when he came into Noa's room?
qa.a: He sat on the floor beside her.

qa.q: How was Noa feeling by the end of the storm, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt calmer and safer; she was counting on her own while still holding his sleeve for comfort.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and how did Yosef fix it?
qa.a: He brushed off her fear from the other room; he then came in, named that she was scared, said sorry for answering too fast and counted with her.

qa.q: If you were Noa, what would you want from a parent during a storm?
qa.a: Someone who comes close, takes the fear seriously and helps you feel steady, even if they got it wrong at first.

grounding: Shows a father repairing a dismissive first reply by naming his child's fear and calmly staying with her.

passage: Observation note, Class 4, week two. Salma joined us from another city only last Monday, yet by Wednesday she had walked up to the kho-kho group and asked, "Can I be on a team?" Today she and Abhinav argued over whose turn it was to chase; voices rose, and she stamped off to the steps. Ten minutes later she was back: "I think you thought it was yours. Let's toss for it." In maths she raised her hand twice and said plainly, "I don't get this bit." No blushing. I have paired her with Abhinav for the craft project; they are already bickering happily.

qa.q: What did Salma ask the kho-kho group?
qa.a: She asked, "Can I be on a team?"

qa.q: How can you tell Salma felt comfortable asking for help in maths?
qa.a: She raised her hand twice and plainly said she didn't get it, with no blushing, so she seemed confident rather than ashamed.

qa.q: What did Salma do after the argument that helped the friendship recover?
qa.a: She cooled off, came back, guessed Abhinav had meant no harm and suggested a toss, so both could keep playing.

qa.q: How might Abhinav see Salma after the quarrel?
qa.a: Abhinav probably sees her as someone who can argue and still be fair, which makes it easy to keep working and even bickering together.

grounding: Shows a school-age child who joins in, recovers from a quarrel by assuming good intent and asks for help openly.

passage:
Tuesday. Vikas said I broke his bat on purpose. I didn't! It cracked on a full toss. I was so angry I went home without saying bye. At dinner I told Mummy everything and asked, "How do I fix it without looking like a baby?" She said just say what happened and offer to help. So after homework I went down with glue and tape. Vikas was sitting on the stairs, looking at the bat. He said, "Sorry I shouted. I think it was already cracked." We taped it together. It looks ugly but it works. Tomorrow we play again.
Hemant

qa.q: What did Hemant take down to the stairs after homework?
qa.a: Glue and tape.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel when Vikas said the bat was broken on purpose?
qa.a: Hemant felt angry and wrongly blamed, because the bat had cracked on a full toss, so Hemant went home without saying bye.

qa.q: What made it easier for Hemant to mend the quarrel?
qa.a: Asking Mummy for help openly, then going down with glue and tape and offering to fix the bat together.

qa.q: What is it like for Vikas when Hemant turns up with glue and tape?
qa.a: Vikas, already sitting with the broken bat, gets an easy chance to say sorry too and admit it was already cracked, so the fight can end.

grounding: Illustrates a child who asks a parent for help without shame and repairs a friendship after a quarrel.

passage: Dust rose over the school ground in Khandwa as Darshan stepped over the line and the kabaddi match was lost. "You gave it away!" Varun yelled. Darshan kicked a stone and walked off towards the well. That evening Varun sat on his roof, still cross, but thinking. Darshan never lost on purpose, and he had been limping since morning. Next day Varun found him by the tea stall. "Your foot okay? Sorry I yelled." Then Varun went to the PT teacher and asked, without looking at his shoes, "Can you teach us to hold the line? We keep losing." Darshan grinned and came along.

qa.q: Where did Varun sit that evening?
qa.a: He sat on his roof, still cross, but thinking.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling on the roof, and what changed his mind?
qa.a: He was still cross about the lost match, but remembering that Darshan had been limping made him think Darshan never lost on purpose.

qa.q: Which choice helped most, and why?
qa.a: Saying sorry first and then asking the PT teacher for help together, because it repaired the friendship and gave both boys a way to improve.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel when Varun asks about his foot?
qa.a: Darshan probably feels relieved and noticed, since his limp is finally seen and the yelling is taken back.

grounding: Shows a child who assumes a friend meant well, recovers after a quarrel and asks an adult for help without shame.

passage: The argument had been about the Lonavala trip: Chetan wanted to go with the older boys from tuition, his mother Bhavna said not this time, and he had slammed his door hard enough to rattle the calendar. Two days of one-word answers followed. Then, on the third night, the power went out across the building and the fan groaned to a stop. Bhavna was lighting a candle in the kitchen when Chetan appeared in the doorway, sweaty, his phone dead. "Ma. Something happened in the group chat. They're all saying I snitched." She pulled out a stool. He sat. The trip didn't come up; they would fight about it again tomorrow, probably. Tonight he talked till the candle was a stub.

qa.q: What happened on the third night?
qa.a: The power went out across the building and the fan groaned to a stop.

qa.q: Why did Chetan come into the kitchen after two days of one-word answers?
qa.a: He was worried and hurt about being called a snitch, and he trusted his mother would listen even while they were still angry about the trip.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do that kept the door open?
qa.a: She pulled out a stool and let him talk, keeping the trip argument separate from his trouble that night.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel when Chetan appears in the doorway?
qa.a: She is likely relieved and touched that he still came to her, even though they may argue about the trip again tomorrow.

grounding: Illustrates a teen who argues for independence yet still comes home to talk when troubled.

passage: Sachin had spent the week arguing with his father about the café job. "Other boys my age work weekends, Papa. You don't trust me." Jagdish kept saying, "Board year first," and Sachin kept rolling his eyes. In the end they settled on Saturdays only, Jagdish grumbling. That Saturday the manager shouted at Sachin in front of customers over a spilled tray and told him to be faster or not come back. On the bus home through Kothrud, Sachin stared at his phone for three stops, then called. "Papa? Can we talk when I get home? Not a lecture. I just need to tell someone." When the bus reached their lane, Jagdish was waiting at the gate with two cups of chai.

qa.q: What did the manager do that Saturday?
qa.a: The manager shouted at Sachin in front of customers over a spilled tray.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling on the bus, and why did he call?
qa.a: He felt humiliated and shaken, and even after a week of arguing he trusted Papa enough to want to talk it through.

qa.q: How could Jagdish support Sachin now without restarting the old fight?
qa.a: He could listen first and hold back any 'I told you so', letting Sachin decide what to do about the job.

qa.q: What is it like for Jagdish to get that call?
qa.a: He is probably worried for Sachin but also glad, because the call shows their bond survived a week of disagreement.

grounding: Shows a teenager who pushes for independence and still turns to a parent when upset.

passage:
"Mum, can I sit?"
"You're allowed in the kitchen, Nandini. Even after yesterday."
"I still think you're unfair about the curfew."
"Noted. Again." Avni kept chopping onions. "What is it?"
"It's Leela. Her family's moving to Guwahati next month. That's why I'm at her place every evening. I just want the time with her."
Avni put the knife down. "Oh. That's sad."
"I didn't tell you because I thought you'd say, 'So say goodbye on the phone.'"
"I might have. I'm glad you told me anyway. Let's talk about Leela and the curfew separately, and find some extra evenings."
"Separately. Okay." Nandini pulled up a stool. "I'm still annoyed with you."
"I know. Pass the tomatoes."

qa.q: Where is Leela's family moving?
qa.a: To Guwahati, next month.

qa.q: Why had Nandini been staying at Leela's place every evening?
qa.a: She is sad that Leela is leaving and wants to spend time with her before the move.

qa.q: What did Avni do that helped the talk go well?
qa.a: She put the knife down, listened, said she was glad Nandini told her and offered to discuss the friend and the curfew separately.

qa.q: How does Avni see the argument after hearing about Leela?
qa.a: Avni seems to understand the late evenings better and is open to finding extra time, while still keeping the curfew as a separate talk.

grounding: Illustrates a teen who argues with a parent yet still comes back to talk, trusting the bond survives disagreement.

passage: Last month Lalit said he wanted the long weekend alone, trekking with his school friends. A year ago I would have heard that as the start of a break-up. This time I noticed the old tightness in my chest, breathed, and said what I actually needed: "Go. Just message me when you reach the top, so I don't spend Sunday imagining cliffs." He laughed and promised. We still fought when he got back, about something silly, and I said something sharp. I called the next morning: "That was unfair of me. I was tired." He admitted he'd been prickly too. I'm Ritu, twenty, and I'm learning that someone needing space is not someone leaving.

qa.q: What did Ritu ask Lalit to do on the trek?
qa.a: To message when reaching the top.

qa.q: What did Ritu feel when Lalit asked for the weekend alone?
qa.a: Ritu felt the old tightness and fear of being left, but calmed it enough to feel secure and say the need plainly.

qa.q: How did Ritu repair the fight after the trek?
qa.a: By calling the next morning, owning the sharp remark and naming tiredness, without blaming Lalit.

qa.q: How might Lalit experience Ritu's reply about the trek?
qa.a: Lalit probably felt trusted rather than guilty, which made it easy to laugh and promise a message.

grounding: Shows a young adult who states a need, allows a partner space and repairs after a fight.

passage: Counsellor's note, Thursday. Simran, second-year, came in to think aloud, not in crisis. Her girlfriend, Chandrika, has started an internship in another city and asked for fewer calls while she settles. Simran said that on the first night she felt panicky and typed three long messages, then deleted them and sent one: "Miss you. Call when you can. I'm okay." She described their fight last week: she said she needed a fixed Sunday call, and they both apologised the next day. She laughed at how ordinary it sounded. What I noticed: she can hold missing Chandrika and trusting her at the same time. Next step: we agreed she would book again only if she wanted to.

qa.q: What message did Simran finally send on the first night?
qa.a: "Miss you. Call when you can. I'm okay."

qa.q: What was Simran feeling on the first night, and how did she handle it?
qa.a: She felt panicky and typed three long messages, but deleted them and sent one calm line, showing she could trust Chandrika despite the fear.

qa.q: How did Simran handle last week's fight?
qa.a: She said clearly that she needed a fixed Sunday call, and both apologised the next day.

qa.q: How might Chandrika experience Simran's short message?
qa.a: Chandrika probably feels free to settle in without guilt, knowing Simran misses her but is okay.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who tolerates a partner's need for space, names a need and repairs after a fight.

passage:
Sunday night. Fought with Kashish today, properly, voices raised in the parking lot. He'd planned a whole trip to Goa with his cousins and told me on Friday like it was a weather report. I said I'm not angry he's going, I'm angry I found out last. He went quiet, which used to make me spiral: is this it, is he done? I didn't text him seventeen times this time. I made dal, watched two episodes and waited. At nine he called. "You're right about telling you earlier. I didn't think." I said I'd been harsh about his cousins too. We're fine. Weirdly, I trust us more after today.
Madhuri

qa.q: When did Kashish tell Madhuri about the trip?
qa.a: On Friday.

qa.q: What did Madhuri feel when Kashish went quiet, and what was different this time?
qa.a: Madhuri felt the old fear that he was done, but stayed calm, did not text seventeen times and trusted him enough to wait.

qa.q: What went well in how the fight was repaired?
qa.a: Madhuri named the real hurt, finding out last, and when Kashish called, both owned their part.

qa.q: How does Kashish seem to see the fight by nine o'clock?
qa.a: He seems to accept that he should have told Madhuri earlier and is willing to own it rather than stay defensive.

grounding: Shows a young adult who says what they need, waits through a partner's silence and repairs after a fight.

passage: Forty minutes before the midnight deadline, the group's slides vanished: someone had saved over the shared file. Manjula watched the other three start blaming each other in the hostel common room, voices climbing. Imran, who had promised to do the final check, went pale, then said, "That was me. I saved the old copy over it. I'm sorry." Nobody spoke. He didn't argue or sulk; he opened his laptop. "I have most of it in my drafts. Give me the charts, I'll rebuild." Manjula noticed how the room cooled. They submitted at 11:58. Walking back, she remembered he had returned her notes on time all term. She wasn't sure she'd have owned up that fast.

qa.q: What time did the group submit?
qa.a: They submitted at 11:58.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling as she walked back?
qa.a: She felt impressed and a little humbled, unsure she would have owned up as fast as Imran did.

qa.q: What could Manjula learn from how Imran handled the mistake?
qa.a: That admitting a mistake quickly and moving straight to fixing it calms a group better than blame.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt when he admitted the mistake?
qa.a: He was likely embarrassed and shaken, since he went pale, but he trusted the group enough to own it and start repairing.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing someone who admits a mistake and repairs it instead of turning it into a crisis.

passage: Rafiq had half expected Jomon to cancel. They'd had a stupid fight on Thursday about splitting a cab fare, and Jomon had gone quiet on the chat. But at seven on Sunday, as the tempo pulled up outside the Koramangala building, there was Jomon with a roll of tape and two samosas. "Said I'd help. So." They carried boxes up four floors. Halfway, Jomon set down a carton. "I was hurt about the cab thing. I also spoke badly. Can we sort it later, over tea?" Rafiq nodded, surprised. Most of his friends either sulked for weeks or pretended nothing had happened. Jomon did neither. By evening the flat was full of boxes, and the fight felt small.

qa.q: What did Jomon bring on Sunday?
qa.a: A roll of tape and two samosas.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel when Jomon turned up and spoke about the fight?
qa.a: Rafiq felt surprised and relieved, because most friends sulked or pretended nothing happened, and Jomon did neither.

qa.q: What small step helped the two friends after the fight?
qa.a: Jomon kept the promise to help and named the hurt, then suggested sorting it later over tea instead of letting it grow.

qa.q: What is it like for Jomon to raise the fight halfway up the stairs?
qa.a: Jomon still feels hurt, yet chooses to say so and own the harsh words, which takes some courage.

grounding: Illustrates a friend noticing someone who keeps a promise and admits hurt without turning a disagreement into a crisis.

passage:
"You're late," Preeti said as Sachin dropped into the canteen chair.
"Twelve minutes. I said four; I'm sorry. The bus broke down near the bridge."
"You could have just said traffic."
"It was the bus. Also, about yesterday. I was short with you when you asked about the notes. That wasn't about you."
Preeti stirred her tea. "Kunal still hasn't spoken to me since our fight in March."
"Kunal treats every argument like a war. I'm not saying I didn't feel stung. I did. I'd rather say it and move on."
"Does it ever just stay stung?"
"Sometimes. Then I say that too."
Preeti smiled despite herself. In two years she had never once had to guess where she stood with Sachin.

qa.q: Why was Sachin late?
qa.a: The bus broke down near the bridge.

qa.q: What does Preeti's smile at the end suggest she feels?
qa.a: She feels reassured and grateful, noticing that with Sachin she never has to guess where she stands.

qa.q: What would you advise Preeti to take from this friendship?
qa.a: That saying a hurt plainly and then moving on keeps a friendship steady, unlike treating every argument as a war.

qa.q: How does Sachin see disagreements?
qa.a: Sachin admits feeling stung sometimes but prefers to say it and move on, rather than letting it become a crisis.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing someone who keeps promises, apologises and repairs rather than letting hurt become a crisis.

passage:
Shreya,
I'm writing this because I'm bad at saying it out loud. Last Sunday, when I finally admitted I'd been dreading your family lunches, not because of your family but because I freeze in big groups, I braced for a cold week. You just said, "Thank you for telling me. Let's leave by three next time." That was it. No sulking, no dragging it into the next argument. It keeps happening: I say the awkward true thing, you listen, we sort it out. In my old relationships I hid almost everything. With you I've started telling you small fears before they grow. I think you've started doing the same with me.
Vijay

qa.q: What did Shreya say when Vijay admitted dreading the lunches?
qa.a: "Thank you for telling me. Let's leave by three next time."

qa.q: How did Vijay feel before and after admitting the truth?
qa.a: Vijay was anxious and braced for a cold week, then felt relieved and steady when Shreya listened without sulking.

qa.q: What does Shreya's response do well?
qa.a: It thanks Vijay for honesty and turns the worry into a simple plan, instead of punishing the confession.

qa.q: How might Shreya see Vijay's growing honesty?
qa.a: Shreya seems to value it and to feel safer sharing small fears in return.

grounding: Shows a partner who feels steady because the other listens and never punishes honesty, making both more open.

passage: You want to know when I knew? It wasn't some big romantic moment. I'm Pankaj, by the way. My wife Sarita and I were fighting about her job offer in Hyderabad, and I said something mean: that she only cared about her career. In my family, a line like that got you three days of silence. Sarita just said, "That hurt. Can you tell me what's under it?" And what was under it was fear, that I'd be the one left behind. She heard that without making me pay for it. We moved together in the end, on a plan we both chose. Now when I'm scared, I say so early. It's easier to be brave next to someone who stays.

qa.q: Where was Sarita's job offer?
qa.a: In Hyderabad.

qa.q: What was Pankaj really feeling under the mean remark?
qa.a: Pankaj was afraid of being left behind, and the mean line covered that fear.

qa.q: Which choice of Sarita's turned the fight around, and why?
qa.a: Saying "That hurt" and asking what was under it, because it invited honesty instead of punishment.

qa.q: What would change if Sarita had answered with three days of silence?
qa.a: Pankaj would likely have hidden the fear, and the move might have become a quiet resentment instead of a shared plan.

grounding: Illustrates a partner who feels safe because the other listens during conflict without punishing honesty.

passage:
Monday: Pallavi had forgotten Pooja's work party again and stood in the doorway rehearsing excuses. Pooja looked up from her laptop. "I was disappointed. I'm not going to hold it over you. Can we use a shared calendar?" Pallavi's shoulders dropped, slowly.

A month on, on a Saturday: Pallavi caught herself telling Pooja about a mistake at work before being asked. It felt strange, almost easy.

qa.q: How is Pooja affected by the teapot confession?
qa.a: Pooja is upset about the loss but glad about the honesty, so she chooses to talk rather than punish.

grounding: Shows over weeks how a partner's consistency and not punishing honesty makes the other steadier and more open.

passage: At the daycare door in Tucson, Camila wrapped both arms around her dad's leg and screamed as Jamal tried to leave. passage: Teacher's note, KG-B. Samir asked me six times this morning, "Is Mumma still at the gate?" At snack he whispered, "Does she love me even when I spill?" passage: In the fishing village near Karwar, Maria stayed so close to her mother Uma's sari that she nearly tripped her while she cleaned fish. "You won't go to the market without me?" "No." Ten minutes later: "You love me, na?" "Still yes." That night Maria was meant to sleep at her cousin's house two lanes away. An hour later her uncle walked her back, sobbing. Uma didn't scold. She sat on the step with her. "Tomorrow we'll try again. I'll walk you over and tell you when I'll come to fetch you."

qa.q: Who walked Maria back that night?
qa.a: Her uncle walked her back, sobbing.

qa.q: What does Maria's repeated "You love me, na?" suggest she is feeling?
qa.a: She seems anxious and unsure, needing to hear again and again that she is loved and that Uma won't leave.

qa.q: How could Uma help Maria manage the next night away?
qa.a: Keep doing what she started: stay calm, sit with her, walk her over and say exactly when she will fetch her.

qa.q: What would change if Uma had called Maria a baby for coming home?
qa.a: Maria would likely feel ashamed and even more afraid of being apart, making the next try harder.

grounding: Illustrates a child seeking constant reassurance and struggling to sleep away, helped by a calm, predictable plan.

passage: "Papá? Are you still there?" Siddiq called from bed for the fourth time, his voice small in the Madrid flat. Diego stopped washing up and went in. "Still here. Still love you." "Even though I kicked the ball at Lucía?" "Even then." Earlier at the park, Siddiq had run back to Diego's bench every few minutes just to touch his knee. Diego didn't tell him to stop being a baby, the way his own father once had. Instead he said, "I'll check on you when the dishes are done, and again when I brush my teeth." He did both times. The calls from bed got fewer.

qa.q: What did Siddiq do at the park?
qa.a: He ran back to Diego's bench every few minutes just to touch his knee.

qa.q: What might Siddiq be worried about when he asks about kicking the ball at Lucía?
qa.a: He seems afraid that doing something wrong could make his father stop loving him.

qa.q: Which choice of Diego's worked, and why?
qa.a: Promising two exact check-ins and keeping both, because it gave Siddiq something predictable to rely on.

qa.q: Why might Diego react differently from his own father?
qa.a: He may remember how it felt to be called a baby and want Siddiq to feel reassured instead of dismissed.

grounding: Shows a child who keeps checking on a parent and asking if he is loved, helped by predictable check-ins rather than dismissal.

passage: When I was ten, beta, at my school in Chennai, my whole world was Elizabeth. One Monday she sat with Grace at lunch and didn't even look up when I passed. I decided at once she hated me. I cried in the washroom and wrote her a furious note. My Ammamma found it in my satchel that evening. She didn't scold. She made me drink warm milk, breathe slowly, and asked, "What else could it mean?" I said maybe Grace was new and alone. Next day Elizabeth came running: "Nirmala, Teacher asked me to sit with the new girl!" I tore up that note. I still keep the habit: calm first, decide later.

qa.q: What did Ammamma find in the satchel?
qa.a: The furious note.

qa.q: What was young Nirmala feeling when Elizabeth sat with Grace?
qa.a: She felt hurt and afraid of being left out, and quickly decided Elizabeth hated her.

qa.q: Which choice in the story mattered most?
qa.a: Calming down with Ammamma and thinking of other meanings before giving the note, which saved the friendship.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth have felt if she had received the furious note?
qa.a: Elizabeth would likely have felt confused and hurt, since she was only sitting with the new girl as asked.

grounding: Shows a child who over-reads a friend's choice and needs help calming the alarm before deciding what it meant.

passage: Jasleen had sent Uday three messages about Saturday's cycle ride from her mother's phone, and nothing came back. By dinner she was sure: Uday was going with the new boy from Block C instead. The storm had knocked out the power, so she couldn't even check again. She pushed her rajma around the plate. Her father lit a candle and asked what was wrong, and it all spilled out, voice wobbling. "Let's slow down," he said. "Breathe with me. Then think of three other reasons someone might not answer." She thought of a dead phone, homework, and the storm. The next morning Uday knocked: "Network was down all night. Ride's on?"

qa.q: What had knocked out the power?
qa.a: The storm.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling at dinner, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was anxious and hurt, sure Uday had chosen someone else; she pushed her food around and her voice wobbled.

qa.q: How did Jasleen's father help her?
qa.a: He helped her breathe and slow down first, then asked her to think of other reasons before deciding what the silence meant.

qa.q: What is it like for Uday the next morning?
qa.a: Uday seems unaware of the worry and simply turns up ready for the ride, since the network had been down.

grounding: Illustrates a child over-reading a friend's silence and needing help to calm the alarm before judging.

passage: At recess in their Dadar school, Sudha saw Manjula laughing with Farida over a shared tiffin, heads close together. Her stomach dropped. Manjula had not saved her a place. All afternoon Sudha answered her in single words and kept her eyes on the blackboard. At home she banged her bag down and told her didi, "Manjula has a new best friend." Didi sat beside her on the bed. "Okay. First, three slow breaths with me. Now: did Manjula say anything unkind?" Sudha thought. "No. She waved at me after." "So you don't know yet. Ask her tomorrow." Next morning Manjula said Farida had forgotten her lunch.

qa.q: What did Sudha bang down at home?
qa.a: Her bag.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling after seeing Manjula laugh with Farida?
qa.a: She felt jealous and afraid of being left out, sure she had been replaced as best friend.

qa.q: What did didi do that helped?
qa.a: She calmed Sudha with slow breaths first, then asked for facts before deciding what Manjula meant.

qa.q: How might Manjula have felt during Sudha's single-word answers?
qa.a: Manjula may have felt puzzled and a little hurt, not knowing why Sudha had gone cold after a friendly wave.

grounding: Shows a child upset by a friend's attention to someone else, helped to calm the alarm before judging the friend.

passage: Every morning at the village school near Sehore, Jaya waited at Anjali-teacher's elbow instead of joining the line. She followed Anjali to the staff room, to the water pot, to the hand pump. The headmaster muttered, "That one just wants attention. Send her off." Anjali watched Jaya's eyes flick to the gate whenever a motorbike passed; her father had gone to work in the city in June. So Anjali gave her a job, ringing the bell for recess, and a promise: "After you ring it, come and tell me." Each week she asked Jaya to carry the register a little farther, first to the next classroom, then alone to the office.

qa.q: What job did Anjali give Jaya?
qa.a: Ringing the bell for recess.

qa.q: What does Anjali seem to think about Jaya's clinginess?
qa.a: She is concerned rather than irritated, seeing Jaya's worry about the gate and her absent father instead of attention-seeking.

qa.q: How could Anjali keep helping Jaya grow more independent?
qa.a: Keep giving small tasks that take her a little farther away, with a steady promise to check back in.

qa.q: What is it like for Jaya when the headmaster wants her sent off?
qa.a: Jaya might feel unwanted and more anxious, since what she needs is steady warmth while her father is away.

grounding: Shows a teacher who sees a clinging child's worry and responds with warmth and small steps towards independence.

passage: Since her grandmother moved back to Porto, Mina had started following Paulo from room to room in their Lisbon flat. She waited outside the bathroom. She asked at every meal, "You're picking me up today, right?" Paulo's brother laughed: "She's playing you. She wants attention." Paulo wasn't so sure. He noticed Mina asked most when her stomach hurt, or when he'd been on the phone a long time. So he started telling her the day's plan each morning, pickup time included, and gave her small missions: buy bread alone at the corner bakery while he waited outside. The first time she came out grinning, holding the loaf like a trophy.

qa.q: What did Mina ask at every meal?
qa.a: "You're picking me up today, right?"

qa.q: What was Paulo thinking when his brother called it attention-seeking?
qa.a: He was doubtful and concerned, noticing that Mina asked most when her stomach hurt, which suggested worry rather than a game.

qa.q: Which choice of Paulo's worked, and why?
qa.a: Telling her the plan each morning and giving small solo missions, because predictability and small wins build confidence.

qa.q: How might Mina feel coming out of the bakery with the loaf?
qa.a: She seems proud and delighted, having managed something alone while knowing Paulo was close.

grounding: Illustrates a parent reading clinginess as worry and answering with warmth and small independence steps.

passage: In the first week at the residential school, Santosh turned up at the warden's office door every evening at seven. "Ma'am, is the phone working? Can I call home?" Then: "Will you be here tomorrow?" Some seniors started calling him the warden's tail. Sharmila, the warden, had seen labels like that stick to kids before. She didn't send him off. Each night she said the same thing: "I'm here till ten, every day except Sunday." She set fixed calls home, Wednesdays and Saturdays. She asked him to help sort letters in the mailroom, beside her at first, then alone for ten minutes while she did rounds. By the third week he came by only on call nights.

qa.q: On which days could Santosh call home?
qa.a: Wednesdays and Saturdays.

qa.q: What was Sharmila thinking when the seniors called Santosh the warden's tail?
qa.a: She was concerned, because she had seen such labels stick to kids, so she chose warmth instead of sending him away.

qa.q: What went right in Sharmila's plan?
qa.a: Same words each night, fixed call days and a small job done alone for longer stretches made the new place feel predictable.

qa.q: What is it like for Santosh in the first week?
qa.a: Santosh seems homesick and unsure, needing to check the phone and whether the warden will still be there.

grounding: Shows a warden who reads a new boarder's clinging as worry and offers steady warmth and small independence steps.
